title: We Won, They Lost
text:
In the early 1970s, Robert Cialdini and his colleagues ran a series of field studies at seven American universities with major college football teams, including Arizona State, Notre Dame, Ohio State and Michigan. They wanted to see how people use the success of a group to which they only loosely belong.

In the first study, observers in introductory psychology classes counted how many students wore clothing with their university's name, team name or insignia on the Monday after each football game. More students wore school clothing after their team had won than after it had lost, and the bigger the win, the more they wore it.

In another study, researchers phoned students and asked them, among other questions, to describe the outcome of a recent game. When their team had won, students were much more likely to use the word we: we won. When it had lost, they more often distanced themselves: they lost. This tendency was strongest when the students had just been made to feel they had failed a test, suggesting that people reach for a winning group's glory most when their own image needs a boost.

Cialdini's team called this basking in reflected glory.
lesson: People rush to share in a team's wins and quietly step away from its losses. Notice who still says we when things go badly; that is real commitment.
people: Robert Cialdini, Richard Borden, Avril Thorne, Marcus Walker, Stephen Freeman, Lloyd Sloan
location: Seven universities in the United States
source: Cialdini, R. B., Borden, R. J., Thorne, A., Walker, M. R., Freeman, S., and Sloan, L. R. (1976). Basking in reflected glory: Three (football) field studies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 34(3), 366-375.
